connection: Production uses async for repository boundaries. The product has no verified requirement to batch-load entries concurrently. Compare sequential and concurrent asynchronous flow in ScratchPad without adding an unrequired batch loader to production.
objectives: Trace LoadSequentialAsync's real await load(id) inside a foreach loop, and explain why each iteration waits for the previous one to finish before starting.
Trace LoadConcurrentAsync's real Task.WhenAll(ids.Select(load)), and explain why every load call starts before any of them necessarily finishes.

Predict, then confirm with EntryBatchLoaderTests's real active/maximum counters, that LoadSequentialAsync never has more than one operation in flight while LoadConcurrentAsync starts all of them immediately.
Explain why the real Clockout(int employeeId) has no equivalent choice to make -- it always operates on exactly one employee, so 'sequential vs concurrent' has never been a real question for it.

visuals.title: Sequential: one await, then the next
visuals.explanation: foreach (int id in ids) results.Add(await load(id)); -- the loop does not call load again until the current await completes.

visuals.title: Concurrent: every operation starts immediately
visuals.explanation: await Task.WhenAll(ids.Select(load)) calls load for every id up front (Select is enumerated eagerly here), then awaits all of them together.

visuals.title: The real test proves it with a counter, not just a description
visuals.explanation: EntryBatchLoaderTests tracks active/maximum concurrent operations: LoadSequentialAsync's maximum never exceeds 1; LoadConcurrentAsync's started count reaches the full batch size before any complete.

visuals.title: Clockout never had this choice to make
visuals.explanation: ClockEntryService.Clockout(int employeeId) processes one employee per call -- there is no batch of employees to run sequentially or concurrently, which is exactly why this session needed a new example.

preQuiz.prompt: In LoadSequentialAsync's foreach (int id in ids) results.Add(await load(id));, does the loop call load for the second id before the first load call has completed?
options: No -- await load(id) suspends the loop until that specific call completes before moving to the next iteration; only one load operation is ever in flight
Yes -- foreach starts every iteration immediately regardless of await
It depends on how many ids there are
preQuiz.explanation: This is exactly what the real EntryBatchLoaderTests.cs proves with its active/maximum counter: LoadSequentialAsync's maximum concurrent count never exceeds 1.

preQuiz.prompt: In LoadConcurrentAsync's Task.WhenAll(ids.Select(load)), when does the second load call happen relative to the first?
options: Effectively immediately -- ids.Select(load) is enumerated eagerly by WhenAll's argument evaluation, calling load for every id before any of the resulting Tasks are awaited together
Only after the first load call's Task completes
Never -- WhenAll only calls load once
preQuiz.explanation: WhenAll takes a collection of already-started Tasks; Select(load) is what starts them all before WhenAll begins waiting for the whole set to finish.

preQuiz.prompt: Why doesn't ClockEntryService.Clockout(int employeeId) ever need to choose between sequential and concurrent execution?
options: It only ever processes one employeeId per call -- 'sequential vs concurrent' is a question about running MULTIPLE independent async operations together, which never applies to a method that handles exactly one
Clockout is always sequential by definition
Clockout cannot be called for multiple employees under any circumstances
preQuiz.explanation: This is precisely why EntryBatchLoader needed to be a new, purpose-built extension -- there was no real multi-item async operation in the source app to study this concept against.

concept.title: Sequential flow starts the next operation later
paragraphs: Awaiting one operation before creating the next is appropriate when order or dependency matters.
The ScratchPad experiment uses controlled delays so start order is visible without changing production behavior.

concept.title: Concurrent flow starts independent work together
paragraphs: Create both tasks first, then await Task.WhenAll when the operations are independent and safe to overlap.
Concurrency is a design decision, not an automatic benefit of writing async.

concept.title: Measure behavior, not wall-clock guesses
paragraphs: The experiment records starts and completions. Tests or controlled gates are more reliable than assuming a specific number of milliseconds.
Production remains single-operation because no batch requirement exists yet.

lab.objective: Compare sequential and concurrent asynchronous flow in ScratchPad without adding an unrequired batch loader to production.
lab.startingCondition: Production uses async for repository boundaries. The product has no verified requirement to batch-load entries concurrently.
steps: In AsyncFlowExperiments.cs, declare a public sealed class named AsyncFlowExperiments.
Add a private static async Task method named LoadAsync with int id and int delayMilliseconds parameters.
At the start of LoadAsync, display a started message containing id.
After the delay, display a completed message containing id.
Add a public async Task method named RunSequentialAsync.
In RunSequentialAsync, display a prediction that operation 2 will start only after operation 1 completes.
Await LoadAsync for operation 2 on the following line.
Add a public async Task method named RunConcurrentAsync.
In RunConcurrentAsync, display a prediction that both operations will start before either completes.
Call LoadAsync for operation 1 without awaiting immediately and store its Task in first.
Call LoadAsync for operation 2 without awaiting immediately and store its Task in second.
Open ScratchPad/Program.cs and preserve earlier session calls.
Await RunConcurrentAsync on the same experiment, then compare the observed ordering with both predictions.
lab.expectedBehavior: ScratchPad demonstrates sequencing versus concurrency without fictional TimeClock batching.
lab.validation: dotnet run --project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad.csproj --configuration Release && dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

expectedFiles.why: Preserve the concurrency comparison outside production.
Keep the lesson synchronized with the cumulative build step.

commit: session-26: teach sequential and concurrent asynchronous flow
review: The lab uses scratchpad because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: If ClockEntryService gained a new method that clocked out an entire list of employees at once, which of EntryBatchLoader's two patterns would it most resemble if implemented naively with a foreach loop and await inside it?
options: LoadSequentialAsync's pattern -- a foreach loop awaiting each Clockout call in turn processes one employee at a time, exactly like LoadSequentialAsync processes one id at a time
LoadConcurrentAsync's pattern -- foreach loops are always concurrent
postQuiz.explanation: A plain foreach with await inside it is definitionally sequential -- this is exactly the shape LoadSequentialAsync demonstrates, and exactly what such a hypothetical batch-Clockout method would need to deliberately change (to Task.WhenAll, LoadConcurrentAsync's pattern) if concurrency were desired instead.

postQuiz.prompt: Why might LoadSequentialAsync sometimes be preferred over LoadConcurrentAsync, even though it is slower in total wall-clock time?
options: When the operations share a resource that cannot safely handle concurrent access (like the real, Singleton-registered ClockEntryRepository's mutable _clockEntries list), running them sequentially avoids race conditions that concurrent execution could introduce
LoadSequentialAsync is always strictly better in every situation
There is never a reason to prefer it
postQuiz.explanation: This connects directly back to the real DI lifetime discussion (Session 20/30): a Singleton-registered, mutable repository is exactly the kind of shared resource where uncontrolled concurrent writes could cause real problems.

postQuiz.prompt: What would happen if LoadConcurrentAsync's ids.Select(load) were changed to ids.Select(load).ToList() before being passed to Task.WhenAll?
options: Functionally very little would change here -- .ToList() would force eager enumeration explicitly, but Select(load) passed directly to WhenAll already causes every load call to run before WhenAll starts waiting
It would make the calls run sequentially instead
It would prevent the calls from starting until awaited
postQuiz.explanation: This is a subtle but real point: LINQ's Select is lazy in general, but passing it directly as WhenAll's argument still causes it to be enumerated (and therefore every load call invoked) immediately, before any awaiting happens -- .ToList() here would be redundant, not a behavior change.

reflections: Why did teaching sequential-vs-concurrent async flow require a brand-new example (EntryBatchLoader) instead of extending something already real in the source app?
What real resource in this codebase (think back to Session 20's DI lifetimes) would make LoadConcurrentAsync's approach risky if applied carelessly?
How does EntryBatchLoaderTests's counter-based proof give you more confidence than simply timing the two methods and comparing durations?
whatBreaks: Changing LoadSequentialAsync's foreach loop to start every load call before awaiting any of them would turn it into a concurrent implementation in disguise, breaking the real active/maximum test's assertion that at most one operation is ever in flight. Changing LoadConcurrentAsync to await each load call individually inside its Select callback (instead of collecting Tasks for WhenAll) would make it behave like LoadSequentialAsync instead, breaking the real started/gate test's assertion that all operations start together.
summary: EntryBatchLoader's real LoadSequentialAsync awaits each operation before starting the next, keeping at most one in flight at a time -- proven by the real test's active/maximum counter, not just asserted. LoadConcurrentAsync starts every operation immediately via Task.WhenAll, proven by the real test's started-count/gate assertion. ClockEntryService.Clockout never faced this choice, because it always processes exactly one employee -- which is exactly why this session needed a new, purpose-built example.
